newsitem.title: USA: SEC votes to curb abuses of offshore offering rule. [CORRECTED 00:05 GMT 10/10/96]
newsitem.headline: SEC votes to curb abuses of offshore offering rule. [CORRECTED 00:05 GMT 10/10/96]

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission voted unanimously on Wednesday for a rule designed to curb problems that have arisen under the agency's six-year-old rule that exempts U.S. corporations from registering offshore offerings.
The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted a rule that requires firms to report offshore sales of equities by U.S. firms within 15 days of the sale, using quarterly reporting Form 8-K.
The SEC also voted to streamline requirements for companies making acquisitions to discourage such firms from going offshore to avoid such standards.

The rules address "problematic practices" that have arisen under Regulation S, the SEC rule that exempts U.S. corporations from registering offshore offerings, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said at today's public meeting on the issues.
"This is one safe harbor with too many pirates in it. We're determined to sweep it clear," Levitt said. He added that today's actions "are not a cure for what ails Reg S."
"The markets are on notice," Levitt said.
"I am committed to addressing these abuses more directly -- the Commission will consider additional initiatives in the near future," Levitt said.
Until today, companies that register with the SEC were not required to disclose sales of unregistered securities in the current or periodic reports they file with the commission.

The result has been to "encourage abusive offshore offering practices," SEC staff said. The SEC voted today to require offshore sales be reported within 15 days of the sale on Form 8-K. Other sales, like private placements, generally must be reported quarterly, under the new rule.
Firms must report the price and amount of securities sold, sale date, type of purchasers and other specific information, SEC said.

The SEC also dropped a requirement that companies supply audited financial statements of businesses they acquire or are likely to acquire when the company they want to acquire has assets totaling more than 10 percent of the total assets of the company seeking to buy it (Corrects to make clear that the previous rule applied when the acquisition represented more than 10 percent of the acquiring company's assets.)
"This requirement has been cited by both domestic and foreign companies as a barrier to conducting a registered U.S. public offering," SEC staff said.
"Companies unable to furnish the financial statements may turn to the offshore markets to raise capital under Regulation S," staff said.

Today's amendments say firms can proceed with registered offerings without supplying financial statements for the businesses they acquired as long as those businesses were no more than half the size of the corporations buying them.
Also, the acquisition must be done after the securities offering or within 74 days of the offering.
SEC also said financial statements must continue to be filed on Form 8-K no later than 75 days after the acquisition is completed.
However, the amendments raise the thresholds for which financial statements are required.
